findings.body:
Removing the `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check lets `deliver()` POST to any caller-supplied URL. A customer-configured endpoint of `http://169.254.169.254/` or `http://127.0.0.1:8300/...` makes this process initiate the request from inside your network; `urlopen` will also follow redirects onto further internal targets.

Restore an egress policy before merging: allow only `https`, resolve and reject private/link-local/metadata addresses, re-validate hosts after redirects (or disable redirects), and keep an explicit host/domain allowlist or a locked-down egress proxy for customer callbacks.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change opens a server-side request forgery (SSRF) path by deleting the only host allowlist on outbound webhook delivery.

## Narrative

`deliver()` previously refused any URL whose hostname was outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. The PR removes that guard and posts directly to the caller-supplied `url` via `urllib.request.urlopen`. Anyone who can influence the webhook URL (customer config, a compromised tenant setting, or a poisoned event pipeline) can make the runner/server issue HTTP requests to:

- link-local cloud metadata (`169.254.169.254`)
- loopback and internal RFC1918 services
- other hosts reachable only from the application network

`urlopen` also follows redirects by default, so a single open redirect on an “external” host is enough to bounce the request deeper into the internal network even if a weaker check were re-added later.

Supporting enterprise customer endpoints is a valid product goal; it needs an egress policy (allowlist/denylist of schemes and hosts/CIDRs, block of link-local and private ranges, no redirects or redirect re-validation, and ideally a dedicated egress proxy), not an unconditional `urlopen` on user input.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The patch deletes ALLOWED_HOSTS and the urlsplit hostname gate that previously raised ValueError, so deliver() now urlopen-POSTs to any caller-supplied URL with no scheme/host/IP checks remaining—an SSRF regression at critical severity.
